claim: Recurrent somatic mutations of H3F3A in aggressive pediatric high-grade gliomas generate K27M or G34R/V mutant histone H3.3.
source: Recurrent somatic mutations of H3F3A in aggressive pediatric high-grade gliomas generate K27M or G34R/V mutant histone H3.3.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established findings about H3F3A mutations in pediatric gliomas.

claim: H3.3-G34R/V mutants are common in tumors with mutations in p53 and ATRX.
source: H3.3-G34R/V mutants are common in tumors with mutations in p53 and ATRX, an H3.3-specific chromatin remodeler.
evidence: This statement in the abstract references known co-occurrence patterns of mutations in pediatric gliomas.

claim: H3-G34R specifically reduces H3K36 tri-methylation in fission yeast.
source: H3-G34R specifically reduces H3K36 tri-methylation and H3K36 acetylation, and mutants show partial transcriptional overlap with set2 deletions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by Western blot data in Figure 1c showing reduced H3K36me3 in H3-G34R cells.

claim: H3-G34R reduces H3K36 acetylation in fission yeast.
source: H3-G34R specifically reduces H3K36 tri-methylation and H3K36 acetylation, and mutants show partial transcriptional overlap with set2 deletions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 1f.

claim: H3-G34R mutants exhibit genomic instability.
source: H3-G34R mutants exhibit genomic instability and increased replication stress, including slowed replication fork restart, although DNA replication checkpoints are functional.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3 showing increased minichromosome loss and lagging chromosomes.

claim: H3-G34R mutants show increased replication stress including slowed replication fork restart.
source: H3-G34R mutants exhibit genomic instability and increased replication stress, including slowed replication fork restart, although DNA replication checkpoints are functional.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 7 showing delayed EdU incorporation and cell proliferation after HU release.

claim: DNA replication checkpoints are functional in H3-G34R mutants.
source: H3-G34R mutants exhibit genomic instability and increased replication stress, including slowed replication fork restart, although DNA replication checkpoints are functional.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5 showing normal γH2A phosphorylation, Chk1 activation, and checkpoint-dependent cell elongation.

claim: H3-G34R mutants are defective for DNA damage repair by homologous recombination.
source: H3-G34R mutants are defective for DNA damage repair by homologous recombination (HR), and have altered HR protein dynamics in both damaged and untreated cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 6f showing reduced HR efficiency and Figure 6e showing epistasis with rad51Δ.

claim: H3-G34R mutants have altered HR protein dynamics in both damaged and untreated cells.
source: H3-G34R mutants are defective for DNA damage repair by homologous recombination (HR), and have altered HR protein dynamics in both damaged and untreated cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 6g and Figure 7d showing altered RPA and Rad52 foci formation.

claim: Fission yeast have three genes that code for a single histone H3 protein.
source: In contrast to the complexity of mammals, where fifteen genes encode three different histone H3 proteins (H3.1, H3.2, H3.3), fission yeast have three genes that code for a single histone H3 protein (Figure 1a) (Matsumoto and Yanagida, 1985).
evidence: This statement cites a published reference (Matsumoto and Yanagida, 1985) and is supported by Figure 1a showing the three H3 genes.

claim: Mammals have fifteen genes that encode three different histone H3 proteins (H3.1, H3.2, H3.3).
source: In contrast to the complexity of mammals, where fifteen genes encode three different histone H3 proteins (H3.1, H3.2, H3.3), fission yeast have three genes that code for a single histone H3 protein (Figure 1a) (Matsumoto and Yanagida, 1985).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about mammalian histone genes.

claim: Sole copy histone H3 and H4 strains maintain histone protein levels similar to those in wild-type strains.
source: These strains maintain histone protein levels similar to those in wild-type strains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b), likely through upregulation of hht2+ and hhf2+ expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b comparing histone levels.

claim: H3-G34R strains are viable at a range of temperatures.
source: These strains are viable at a range of temperatures and appear to have normal chromosomal integrity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d,e).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: H3-G34R strains appear to have normal chromosomal integrity.
source: These strains are viable at a range of temperatures and appear to have normal chromosomal integrity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d,e).
evidence: This claim is supported by PFGE data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e showing intact chromosomes.

claim: In mammalian cells, ectopic expression of H3.3G34R reduced K36me2/3 methylation on the mutant histone tail.
source: In mammalian cells, ectopic expression of H3.3G34R reduced K36me2/3 methylation on the mutant histone tail (Lewis et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement cites a published reference (Lewis et al., 2013).

claim: Five enzymes can methylate H3K36 in mammals, with only SETD2 responsible for H3K36me3.
source: Five enzymes can methylate H3K36 in mammals, with only SETD2 responsible for H3K36me3 (Edmunds et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement cites a published reference (Edmunds et al., 2008).

claim: In fission yeast, a single enzyme (Set2) performs all methylation on H3K36.
source: In fission yeast, a single enzyme, Set2, performs all methylation on H3K36 (Morris et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement cites a published reference (Morris et al., 2005).

claim: H3K36me3 was markedly reduced in H3-G34R compared to H3-WT cell extracts.
source: Using these antibodies, we found that H3K36me3 was markedly reduced in H3-G34R compared to H3-WT cell extracts, but that H3K36me2 levels were unchanged (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1c showing reduced H3K36me3 signal in H3-G34R.

claim: H3K36me2 levels were unchanged in H3-G34R compared to H3-WT cell extracts.
source: Using these antibodies, we found that H3K36me3 was markedly reduced in H3-G34R compared to H3-WT cell extracts, but that H3K36me2 levels were unchanged (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1c showing similar H3K36me2 signal in H3-WT and H3-G34R.

claim: K36me2 is elevated in H3-G34R cells.
source: As we observed that binding of the H3K36me2 antibody is reduced ~10 fold on G34R peptides, these results suggest that K36me2 is elevated in H3-G34R cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combination of antibody binding data (Figure 1b) and Western blot results (Figure 1c).

claim: Set2 function is altered in H3-G34R cells, with specific reduction of H3K36me3 and retention/accumulation of H3K36me2.
source: Thus Set2 function is altered in H3-G34R cells, with specific reduction of H3K36me3 and retention/ accumulation of H3K36me2.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Western blot and antibody binding data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Endogenously tagged Set2-FLAG protein levels were similar in H3-WT and H3-G34R cells.
source: Since endogenously tagged Set2-FLAG protein levels were similar in H3-WT and H3-G34R cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h), the reduction in H3K36me3 is not caused by a loss of set2+ expression in H3-G34R cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1h.

claim: Set2-FLAG recruitment to chromatin was not reduced in H3-G34R cells.
source: Additionally, chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) analysis revealed that Set2-FLAG recruitment to chromatin was not reduced in H3-G34R cells (Figure 1d), suggesting that the H3-G34R mutation hinders Set2 activity but not access to K36.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data in Figure 1d showing similar Set2-FLAG enrichment at act1+ and clr4+ loci.

claim: The H3-G34R mutation hinders Set2 activity but not access to K36.
source: Additionally, chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) analysis revealed that Set2-FLAG recruitment to chromatin was not reduced in H3-G34R cells (Figure 1d), suggesting that the H3-G34R mutation hinders Set2 activity but not access to K36.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ChIP data showing normal Set2 recruitment but reduced methylation.

claim: Set2 overexpression restored K36me2 and me3 in H3-WT set2Δ strains.
source: Western analysis of extracts prepared from cells that overexpress Set2 showed that pSet2-FLAG restored K36me2 and me3 in H3-WT set2Δ strains but was able to generate only low levels of H3K36me3 in both H3-G34R and H3-G34R set2Δ cells (Figure 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1e.

claim: Set2 overexpression was able to generate only low levels of H3K36me3 in H3-G34R cells.
source: Western analysis of extracts prepared from cells that overexpress Set2 showed that pSet2-FLAG restored K36me2 and me3 in H3-WT set2Δ strains but was able to generate only low levels of H3K36me3 in both H3-G34R and H3-G34R set2Δ cells (Figure 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1e.

claim: The H3-G34R mutation reduces Set2 activity on the H3 tail, leading to a specific reduction in tri-methylation of H3K36.
source: Thus the H3-G34R mutation reduces Set2 activity on the H3 tail, leading to a specific reduction in tri-methylation of H3K36, and this effect cannot be bypassed by overexpression of Set2.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Set2 overexpression data in Figure 1e.

claim: H3K36 is regulated by acetylation in addition to methylation.
source: In addition to methylation of H3K36, this residue is also regulated by acetylation (Morris et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement cites a published reference (Morris et al., 2007).

claim: Acetylation of K36 on histone H3 was greatly reduced in H3-G34R strains.
source: These studies showed acetylation of K36 on histone H3 was greatly reduced in H3-G34R strains and somewhat reduced in set2Δ.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 1f.

claim: There was a slight upregulation of H3K18 acetylation in H3-G34R.
source: Additionally, there was a slight upregulation of H3K18 acetylation and possibly enhanced K27 acetylation in H3-G34R, although K27 acetylation in H3-WT was highly variable.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 1f.

claim: set2Δ cells showed a slight reduction of H4 K16 acetylation.
source: set2Δ cells showed more widespread changes, with a slight reduction of H4 K16 acetylation, some induction of H3K9 and K18 acetylation and a marked increase in H3K14 acetylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 1f.

claim: set2Δ cells showed a marked increase in H3K14 acetylation.
source: set2Δ cells showed more widespread changes, with a slight reduction of H4 K16 acetylation, some induction of H3K9 and K18 acetylation and a marked increase in H3K14 acetylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 1f.

claim: H3K36me3 and H3K36 acetylation have been shown to be cell cycle regulated.
source: H3K36me3 and H3K36 acetylation have been shown to be cell cycle regulated (Li et al., 2013; Pai et al., 2014), with K36me3 accumulating in G1 and early-mid S phase.
evidence: This statement cites published references (Li et al., 2013; Pai et al., 2014).

claim: K36me3 accumulates in G1 and early-mid S phase.
source: H3K36me3 and H3K36 acetylation have been shown to be cell cycle regulated (Li et al., 2013; Pai et al., 2014), with K36me3 accumulating in G1 and early-mid S phase.
evidence: This statement cites published references (Li et al., 2013; Pai et al., 2014).

claim: Levels of H3K36me3 were reduced in H3-G34R cells compared to H3-WT at all stages of the cell cycle.
source: Although levels of H3K36me3 were reduced in H3-G34R cells compared to H3-WT at all stages of the cell cycle (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,b,c), H3K36me3 did accumulate in both H3-WT and H3-G34R cells synchronized in G1, indicative that the G34R mutation does not override cell cycle control of Set2 function.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a showing reduced H3K36me3 at different cell cycle stages.

claim: H3K36me3 accumulates in both H3-WT and H3-G34R cells synchronized in G1.
source: Although levels of H3K36me3 were reduced in H3-G34R cells compared to H3-WT at all stages of the cell cycle (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,b,c), H3K36me3 did accumulate in both H3-WT and H3-G34R cells synchronized in G1, indicative that the G34R mutation does not override cell cycle control of Set2 function.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,c.

claim: The G34R mutation does not override cell cycle control of Set2 function.
source: Although levels of H3K36me3 were reduced in H3-G34R cells compared to H3-WT at all stages of the cell cycle (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,b,c), H3K36me3 did accumulate in both H3-WT and H3-G34R cells synchronized in G1, indicative that the G34R mutation does not override cell cycle control of Set2 function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that H3K36me3 still accumulates in G1 in H3-G34R cells.

claim: H3K36me2 levels are higher throughout the cell cycle in H3-G34R compared to H3-WT cells.
source: Additionally, this experiment also demonstrates that H3K36me2 levels are higher throughout the cell cycle in H3-G34R compared to H3-WT cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,c.

claim: Cells that lack the H3K36 methyltransferase Set2 show widespread transcriptional upregulation in fission yeast.
source: Cells that lack the H3K36 methyltransferase Set2 or that express a mutant of Set2 that allows only di-methylation of K36 show a similar widespread transcriptional upregulation in fission yeast (Suzuki et al., 2016; Matsuda et al., 2015), suggesting that H3K36me2 is not sufficient for silencing.
evidence: This statement cites published references (Suzuki et al., 2016; Matsuda et al., 2015).

claim: H3K36me2 is not sufficient for silencing.
source: Cells that lack the H3K36 methyltransferase Set2 or that express a mutant of Set2 that allows only di-methylation of K36 show a similar widespread transcriptional upregulation in fission yeast (Suzuki et al., 2016; Matsuda et al., 2015), suggesting that H3K36me2 is not sufficient for silencing.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited studies showing that cells with only K36me2 have transcriptional upregulation.

claim: In set2Δ, 753 genes were upregulated and 149 genes downregulated.
source: In genome-wide RNA-Seq analyses, set2Δ had many transcripts with altered regulation (753 genes were up and 149 genes downregulated) (Figure 2a,b) in an organism with ~5100 protein coding genes and ~1500 non coding RNAs (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 2a,b and Supplementary file 3.

claim: The H3-G34R mutant showed repression of 69 genes and upregulation of 172 genes.
source: Unexpectedly, the H3-G34R mutant showed more mild transcriptional effects (repression of 69 genes and upregulation of 172 genes).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 2a,b and Supplementary file 3.

claim: 143 genes were deregulated in both H3-G34R and set2Δ cells.
source: 143 genes were deregulated in both H3-G34R and set2Δ cells: 97 were coordinately regulated, with 9 genes downregulated, and 88 genes upregulated in both set2Δ and H3-G34R (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 2b.

claim: 88 genes were upregulated in both set2Δ and H3-G34R.
source: 143 genes were deregulated in both H3-G34R and set2Δ cells: 97 were coordinately regulated, with 9 genes downregulated, and 88 genes upregulated in both set2Δ and H3-G34R (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 2b.

claim: Transcripts that are differentially regulated between H3-G34R and set2Δ map to regions adjacent to subtelomeric regions of chromosome 1 and 2.
source: As can be seen on chromosome-wide plots (Figure 2c,d), transcripts that are differentially regulated between H3-G34R and set2Δ map to regions adjacent to subtelomeric regions of chromosome 1 and 2 (ST or sub-subtelomeric domains [Matsuda et al., 2015; Buchanan et al., 2009]), which are not heterochromatic and are normally expressed at low levels (Mata et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 2c,d showing chromosome-wide expression patterns.

claim: Set2 represses antisense transcription in both S. cerevisiae and S. pombe.
source: Set2 has also been shown in both S. cerevisiae and S. pombe to repress antisense transcription (Nicolas et al., 2007; Shim et al., 2012; Venkatesh et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement cites published references (Nicolas et al., 2007; Shim et al., 2012; Venkatesh et al., 2016).

claim: 318 antisense transcripts were differentially regulated in set2Δ compared to H3-WT cells.
source: Focusing on just these antisense transcripts, of which there are 635 in fission yeast, we found that, compared to H3-WT cells, 318 were differentially regulated in set2Δ, and 62 in H3-G34R mutants, with the vast majority being upregulated (313 and 57, respectively) (Figure 2f).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 2f.

claim: 62 antisense transcripts were differentially regulated in H3-G34R mutants compared to H3-WT cells.
source: Focusing on just these antisense transcripts, of which there are 635 in fission yeast, we found that, compared to H3-WT cells, 318 were differentially regulated in set2Δ, and 62 in H3-G34R mutants, with the vast majority being upregulated (313 and 57, respectively) (Figure 2f).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 2f.

claim: 47 antisense transcripts were targeted by both Set2 and H3-G34R.
source: 47 antisense transcripts were targeted by both Set2 and H3-G34R, and 43 of these accumulated in both mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 2f.

claim: Trimethylation of K36 may repress antisense transcription.
source: Therefore H3-G34R cells, similar to set2Δ cells, upregulate antisense transcripts, indicative that trimethylation of K36 may repress antisense transcription.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that both H3-G34R and set2Δ show upregulation of antisense transcripts.

claim: Repression of sub-subtelomeric domains may be linked to dimethylation of K36 in H3-G34R.
source: We conclude that suppression of antisense gene transcription appears linked to trimethylation of K36, as it is reduced in both H3-G34R and set2Δ, and that repression of sub-subtelomeric domains may be linked to dimethylation of K36 in H3-G34R, as it is abolished in set2Δ or compound set2Δ H3-G34R mutants that lack dimethylation of K36.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential regulation of sub-subtelomeric genes in H3-G34R versus set2Δ.

claim: Heterochromatin is intact in H3-G34R mutants.
source: Transcript levels were similar in H3-G34R and H3-WT, suggesting that heterochromatin is intact in H3-G34R mutants, whereas set2Δ showed a slight upregulation in subtelomeric tlh transcripts.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a showing similar transcript levels at heterochromatic loci.

claim: H3-G34R mutation had no impact on H3K9 methylation at heterochromatic regions.
source: As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and c, H3-G34R mutation had no impact on H3K9 methylation or Swi6HP1 recruitment to heterochromatic regions (Ekwall et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b showing similar H3K9me2 levels.

claim: H3-G34R mutation had no impact on Swi6HP1 recruitment to heterochromatic regions.
source: As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and c, H3-G34R mutation had no impact on H3K9 methylation or Swi6HP1 recruitment to heterochromatic regions (Ekwall et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c showing similar Swi6 enrichment.

claim: H3-G34R mutation showed no change in Cnp1 recruitment to centromeric central core sequences.
source: ChIP against Cnp1 (Castillo et al., 2007), the fission yeast CENP-A protein that underlies and supports kinetochore assembly, showed no change in Cnp1 recruitment to centromeric central core sequences in H3-G34R mutant cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The architecture of centromeric and telomeric heterochromatin is intact in H3-G34R cells.
source: Together, the lack of apparent effect on kinetochore or heterochromatic structures indicates that the architecture of centromeric and telomeric heterochromatin is intact in H3-G34R cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ChIP and transcript data showing normal heterochromatin markers.

claim: H3-G34R cells lost minichromosomes at an elevated frequency (3.5%).
source: Interestingly, we found that H3-G34R cells lost minichromosomes at an elevated frequency (3.5%), while minichromosome loss in set2Δ was not significantly upregulated (1.6%).
evidence: This claim is supported by minichromosome loss assay data in Figure 3a.

claim: Minichromosome loss in set2Δ was not significantly upregulated (1.6%).
source: Interestingly, we found that H3-G34R cells lost minichromosomes at an elevated frequency (3.5%), while minichromosome loss in set2Δ was not significantly upregulated (1.6%).
evidence: This claim is supported by minichromosome loss assay data in Figure 3a.

claim: Chromosomes mis-segregated in 7.4% of H3-G34R cells.
source: Counting only late anaphase cells (spindle >10 microns), we found that chromosomes mis-segregated in 7.4% of H3-G34R cells compared to 0.9% in H3-WT, 1.3% in set2Δ and 25.6% in clr4Δ cells that lack heterochromatin.
evidence: This claim is supported by lagging chromosome analysis data in Figure 3b.

claim: ~38% of H3-G34R cells showed stretching of DNA or aberrantly positioned DNA on mid to late anaphase spindles compared with ~14% of H3-WT cells.
source: Furthermore, in cells synchronized using an nda3-KM311 early mitotic block and release (Hiraoka et al., 1984), and stained for tubulin and DNA, ~38% of H3-G34R cells showed stretching of DNA or aberrantly positioned DNA on mid to late anaphase spindles compared with ~14% of H3-WT cells (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by chromosome segregation analysis data in Figure 3c.

claim: H3-G34R cells exhibit elevated chromosomal instability, which is independent of heterochromatin or kinetochore defects.
source: Together, these data show that the H3-G34R cells exhibit elevated chromosomal instability, which is independent of heterochromatin or kinetochore defects.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the chromosome stability data in Figure 3 and the heterochromatin/kinetochore data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: H3K36me3 and H3K36 acetylation are modifications that are linked to DNA damage responses.
source: Since H3-G34R cells show increased chromosomal instability, and are reduced in histone H3 K36 acetylation and tri-methylation, which are modifications that are linked to DNA damage responses (Pai et al., 2014; Pfister et al., 2014; Jha and Strahl, 2014; Li et al., 2013), we tested H3-G34R strains for sensitivity to DNA damaging agents.
evidence: This statement cites published references (Pai et al., 2014; Pfister et al., 2014; Jha and Strahl, 2014; Li et al., 2013).

claim: Chronic exposure to HU, CPT, and MMS resulted in significant sensitivity of H3-G34R cells compared with H3-WT cells.
source: We found that chronic exposure to each genotoxin resulted in significant sensitivity of H3-G34R cells compared with H3-WT cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by serial dilution assay data in Figure 4a.

claim: H3-G34R mutants showed no sensitivity to gamma irradiation or bleomycin.
source: Conversely, when H3-G34R and H3-WT cells were exposed to gamma irradiation (γIR) or bleomycin, two replication-independent genotoxins, H3-G34R mutants showed no sensitivity, whereas set2Δ cells were sensitive to γIR and bleomycin (Figure 4b and c) as seen previously (Pai et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 4b,c showing similar viability of H3-WT and H3-G34R after IR or bleomycin treatment.

claim: set2Δ cells were sensitive to γIR and bleomycin.
source: Conversely, when H3-G34R and H3-WT cells were exposed to gamma irradiation (γIR) or bleomycin, two replication-independent genotoxins, H3-G34R mutants showed no sensitivity, whereas set2Δ cells were sensitive to γIR and bleomycin (Figure 4b and c) as seen previously (Pai et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 4b,c and cites a published reference (Pai et al., 2014).

claim: H3-G34R cells appear selectively sensitive to agents that generate DNA replication stress.
source: Thus H3-G34R, but not set2Δ cells appear selectively sensitive to agents that generate DNA replication stress.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential sensitivity patterns shown in Figure 4.

claim: Additive growth defects were seen for set2Δ H3-G34R double mutants on CPT and MMS, but not with HU.
source: Additive growth defects were seen for set2Δ H3-G34R double mutants on CPT and MMS, but not with HU (Figure 4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by serial dilution assay data in Figure 4d.

claim: Set2 overexpression fully compensated for set2Δ growth defects on damaging agents.
source: Whereas pSet2-FLAG overexpression fully compensated for set2Δ growth defects on damaging agents, no growth advantage was conferred on H3-G34R cells (Figure 4e).
evidence: This claim is supported by serial dilution assay data in Figure 4e.

claim: Set2 overexpression conferred no growth advantage on H3-G34R cells on damaging agents.
source: Whereas pSet2-FLAG overexpression fully compensated for set2Δ growth defects on damaging agents, no growth advantage was conferred on H3-G34R cells (Figure 4e).
evidence: This claim is supported by serial dilution assay data in Figure 4e.

claim: H3-G34R or set2Δ strains showed no differences in γH2A phosphorylation levels compared to H3-WT after HU or MMS treatment.
source: Western analyses of cells treated with HU or MMS showed no differences in γH2A phosphorylation levels in H3-G34R or set2Δ strains compared to H3-WT, indicative that the function of upstream kinases is not perturbed in H3-G34R cells (Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 5b.

claim: Chk1 was efficiently activated by MMS treatment in H3-G34R cells.
source: Next, we monitored phosphorylation-related mobility shifts of Chk1-HA and found that Chk1 was efficiently activated by MMS treatment in H3-G34R cells, suggesting that DNA damage checkpoint signaling was normal (Figure 5c) (Walworth and Bernards, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 5c showing Chk1-HA mobility shift.

claim: H3-G34R showed no accumulation of RPA foci after HU release, supporting that the Cds1 pathway is functional.
source: In contrast to the 'flares' of RPA seen in cds1Δ after release, H3-G34R showed no accumulation of RPA foci (Figure 5d), supporting that the Cds1 pathway is functional in H3-G34R mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5d showing no RPA flares in H3-G34R.

claim: H3-G34R cds1Δ and H3-G34R chk1Δ double mutants arrested normally as elongated cells after HU treatment.
source: H3-G34R cds1Δ and H3-G34R chk1Δ double mutants also arrested normally as elongated cells, suggesting that both checkpoints are intact in H3-G34R (Figure 5e).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell elongation data in Figure 5e.

claim: DNA damage checkpoint signaling appears to be functional in H3-G34R cells.
source: In summary, DNA damage checkpoint signaling appears to be functional in H3-G34R cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the checkpoint assay data presented in Figure 5.

claim: H3-G34R cells do not rely on ORC to recover from HU-imposed replication stress.
source: Intriguingly, unlike orp1-4 brc1Δ which die due to severe mitotic defects (Bass et al., 2012) (red bars, Figure 6b), we found that orp1-4 H3-G34R survive. Thus, H3-G34R cells do not rely on ORC to recover from HU-imposed replication stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by viability assay data in Figure 6b showing survival of orp1-4 H3-G34R after HU treatment.

claim: H3-G34R mutants with rad18Δ or ubc13Δ show synergistic sensitivity to MMS.
source: H3-G34R mutants with either of these mutations show synergistic sensitivity to MMS, suggesting that the PRR pathways are functional in H3-G34R cells (Figure 6c).
evidence: This claim is supported by serial dilution assay data in Figure 6c.

claim: H3-G34R showed synergistic defects with ku70Δ when assessed on MMS.
source: H3-G34R showed synergistic defects with ku70Δ when assessed on MMS compared with either single mutant, indicating that NHEJ is functional in H3-G34R cells (Figure 6d).
evidence: This claim is supported by serial dilution assay data in Figure 6d.

claim: H3-G34R rad51Δ double mutants showed epistasis with single mutants when plated on MMS.
source: In contrast to mutations with PRR or NHEJ proteins, H3-G34R rad51Δ double mutants showed epistasis with single mutants when plated on MMS (Figure 6e).
evidence: This claim is supported by serial dilution assay data in Figure 6e.

claim: H3-G34R cells have a defective HR pathway.
source: This suggests that H3-G34R cells have a defective HR pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the epistasis data with rad51Δ shown in Figure 6e.

claim: H3-G34R and set2Δ strains showed ~35% HR efficiency compared to H3-WT cells.
source: As expected, rad51Δ cells were very defective with HR rates of only ~3% of H3-WT cells. H3-G34R and set2Δ strains were also defective (~35% efficiency) and the double H3-G34R set2Δ mutant showed an even stronger defect, with a 90% drop in HR efficiency.
evidence: This claim is supported by HR assay data in Figure 6f.

claim: The double H3-G34R set2Δ mutant showed a 90% drop in HR efficiency.
source: As expected, rad51Δ cells were very defective with HR rates of only ~3% of H3-WT cells. H3-G34R and set2Δ strains were also defective (~35% efficiency) and the double H3-G34R set2Δ mutant showed an even stronger defect, with a 90% drop in HR efficiency.
evidence: This claim is supported by HR assay data in Figure 6f.

claim: Both H3-G34R and set2Δ reduce HR efficiency but via distinct mechanisms.
source: Thus both H3-G34R and set2Δ reduce HR efficiency but via distinct mechanisms, as additive defects are seen in the set2Δ H3-G34R double mutant.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the additive HR defects in the double mutant shown in Figure 6f.

claim: H3-G34R had an extended doubling time of 201 min (±4 min) compared to 180 min (±10 min) for H3-WT.
source: We measured the generation time during exponential growth and found that H3-G34R had an extended doubling time of 201 min (±4 min) compared to 180 min (±10 min) for H3-WT, and 194 min (±8 min) for set2Δ in rich media at 32°C.
evidence: This claim is based on measurements of cell doubling times during exponential growth.

claim: S phase is prolonged in H3-G34R cells and not completed until 140–160 min after release from G1 arrest.
source: H3-WT cells have completed DNA synthesis by 80–100 min, whereas S phase is prolonged in H3-G34R cells and not completed until 140–160 min after release.
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 showing delayed completion of S phase.

claim: H3-G34R cells showed increased numbers of RPA and Rad52 foci compared to H3-WT.
source: Consistent with enhanced replication stress in H3-G34R cells, H3-G34R cells showed increased numbers of RPA and Rad52 foci (Bass et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6g.

claim: Fewer MMS-treated H3-G34R cells showed Rad51 and Rad52 foci compared with H3-WT and set2Δ.
source: Surprisingly however, fewer MMS-treated H3-G34R cells showed Rad51 and Rad52 foci compared with H3-WT and set2Δ.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6g.

claim: The reduction in Rad51 and Rad52 foci was not linked to a change in protein expression.
source: The reduction in foci was not linked to a change in protein expression as Rad51 and Rad52 protein levels were similar in MMS treated H3-WT and H3-G34R cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 6—figure supplement 3b.

claim: Rad52 foci co-localized with RPA.
source: Additionally, Rad52 foci co-localized with RPA, suggesting that Rad52 foci occur at sites of DNA damage (Figure 6—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data in Figure 6—figure supplement 3c.

claim: H3-G34R cells exhibit anaphase bridges, with RPA marking ultrafine bridges between DAPI staining masses.
source: To address this, we monitored RPA localization in anaphase cells following cdc10 block and release, and found that H3-G34R cells exhibit anaphase bridges, with RPA marking ultrafine bridges between DAPI staining masses (Figure 6—figure supplement 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6—figure supplement 3d.

claim: Chromosome segregation defects in H3-G34R cells are linked to the delayed resolution of replication intermediates.
source: This supports that chromosome segregation defects in H3-G34R cells are linked to the delayed resolution of replication intermediates.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation of RPA-marked anaphase bridges in H3-G34R cells.

claim: H3-G34R cells delay proliferation for 3 hr after HU release rather than 2 hr for H3-WT.
source: While H3-G34R do delay proliferation for longer than H3-WT (3 hr rather than 2 hr), the proliferation rates at later time points appear similar.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation data in Figure 7a.

claim: De novo DNA synthesis is initially delayed in H3-G34R cells after HU release.
source: Interestingly, de novo DNA synthesis is initially delayed in H3-G34R cells but at later time points after HU release, the rates of DNA synthesis appear similar in H3-WT and H3-G34R cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation data in Figure 7b.

claim: γH2A signal accumulated more slowly in H3-G34R cells during MMS treatment and peaked at 45 min into the recovery period.
source: Surprisingly, γH2A signal accumulated more slowly in H3-G34R cells, and peaked at 45 min into the recovery period, at higher levels than seen in H3-WT cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 7c showing kinetics of γH2A accumulation.

claim: γH2A remained intensely phosphorylated at later time points in H3-G34R cells compared with H3-WT cells during recovery from MMS.
source: On recovery from MMS, γH2A remained intensely phosphorylated at later time points in H3-G34R cells compared with H3-WT cells (see Figure 7c).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 7c.

claim: Rad52 foci accumulated faster in MMS treated H3-WT cells than H3-G34R.
source: Similar to γH2A, Rad52 foci accumulated faster in MMS treated H3-WT cells than H3-G34R, even though more Rad52 foci were present in untreated H3-G34R cells than in H3-WT (Figure 7d).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 7d showing kinetics of Rad52 foci formation.

claim: Rad52 foci continued to accumulate in H3-G34R during recovery from MMS, peaking at 90 min following release.
source: During recovery, H3-WT cells with Rad52 foci dropped to ~50% by 180 mins while Rad52 foci continued to accumulate in H3-G34R, peaking at 90 min following release, before dropping.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 7d.

claim: The kinetics of DNA damage response are different between H3-WT and H3-G34R cells.
source: These data suggest that the kinetics of DNA damage response are different between H3-WT and H3-G34R cells, with H3-G34R mutants showing a slower induction of damage response, as well as accumulation of recombination proteins at later timepoints following damage, which may contribute to the HR-mediated repair defect in H3-G34R mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the kinetics data presented in Figure 7.

claim: H3-G34R mutants show a slower induction of damage response.
source: These data suggest that the kinetics of DNA damage response are different between H3-WT and H3-G34R cells, with H3-G34R mutants showing a slower induction of damage response, as well as accumulation of recombination proteins at later timepoints following damage, which may contribute to the HR-mediated repair defect in H3-G34R mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the kinetics data presented in Figure 7.

claim: G34R mutations are only found in H3.3, primarily in one of two H3.3 genes (H3F3A).
source: Notably, G34R mutations are only found in H3.3, primarily in one of two H3.3 genes (H3F3A) and not in the replication coupled H3 proteins H3.1 and H3.2, which are encoded by a total of 13 genes.
evidence: This is a statement of known mutation patterns in pediatric gliomas.

claim: G34R mutations are commonly found in tumors additionally mutant for the tumor suppressor p53 and ATRX.
source: G34R mutations are commonly found in tumors additionally mutant for the tumor suppressor p53 and ATRX, a chromatin remodeler involved specifically in nucleosomal deposition of the H3.3 variant histone at telomeres and pericentric heterochromatin (Goldberg et al., 2010; Lewis et al., 2010; Drané et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement cites published references (Goldberg et al., 2010; Lewis et al., 2010; Drané et al., 2010).

claim: ATRX is a chromatin remodeler involved specifically in nucleosomal deposition of the H3.3 variant histone at telomeres and pericentric heterochromatin.
source: G34R mutations are commonly found in tumors additionally mutant for the tumor suppressor p53 and ATRX, a chromatin remodeler involved specifically in nucleosomal deposition of the H3.3 variant histone at telomeres and pericentric heterochromatin (Goldberg et al., 2010; Lewis et al., 2010; Drané et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement cites published references (Goldberg et al., 2010; Lewis et al., 2010; Drané et al., 2010).

claim: G34R nucleosomes had reduced K36me2/3 on the same H3.3 tail.
source: One published study showed G34R nucleosomes had reduced K36me2/3 on the same H3.3 tail (Lewis et al., 2013), suggesting a potential role in regulating H3K36 methylation in gliomas.
evidence: This statement cites a published reference (Lewis et al., 2013).

claim: Mutations in SETD2 have frequently been identified in pHGG.
source: Furthermore, mutations in SETD2, the enzyme that performs H3K36 di- to tri-methylation in mammals (Edmunds et al., 2008), have also frequently been identified in pHGG (Fontebasso et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement cites published references (Edmunds et al., 2008; Fontebasso et al., 2013).

claim: SETD2 mutations are not found in conjunction with histone mutations.
source: However, SETD2 mutations are not found in conjunction with histone mutations, suggesting the importance of disruption of the H3K36me3/ SETD2 axis in cortical pHGG.
evidence: This is a statement about mutation co-occurrence patterns in pediatric gliomas.

claim: H3.3 is deposited into regions of constitutive heterochromatin including repetitive telomeric and pericentromeric domains.
source: H3.3 is deposited into regions of constitutive heterochromatin including repetitive telomeric and pericentromeric domains, and at regions of high transcriptional activity through the activity of specialized chaperones (reviewed in Kallappagoudar et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement cites a review (Kallappagoudar et al., 2015).

claim: Clearance of γH2A.X foci in human cells that lack H3K36me3 due to deletion of SETD2 is delayed.
source: We note that consistent with our findings, clearance of γH2A.X foci in human cells that lack H3K36me3 due to deletion of SETD2 is delayed (Hacker et al., 2016), and such cells are defective for HR and exhibit genomic instability (Pfister et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement cites published references (Hacker et al., 2016; Pfister et al., 2014).

claim: Human cells that lack H3K36me3 due to deletion of SETD2 are defective for HR and exhibit genomic instability.
source: We note that consistent with our findings, clearance of γH2A.X foci in human cells that lack H3K36me3 due to deletion of SETD2 is delayed (Hacker et al., 2016), and such cells are defective for HR and exhibit genomic instability (Pfister et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement cites a published reference (Pfister et al., 2014).
